summary: A response to RFC 607's comments on the File Transfer Protocol. It is one of several notes on FTP changes, along with RFCs 624, 542 and 640.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone made suggestions about the file transfer rules. This note answers them.

subtitle: Point-by-point answers to RFC 607's suggested changes to the early File Transfer Protocol.

tldr.problem: RFC 607 raised many sticky issues in the early FTP, from passive mode to reply codes and mail.
tldr.mechanism: The authors answer its numbered paragraphs one by one, agreeing on some (four-character commands, discarding data after the last end-of-record) and disagreeing on others (multi-line replies, a simple 2xx success rule).
tldr.outcome: They propose clarifications such as the order of handshaking, a 15-second minimum wait, "must" for success replies, dropping the 331 reply, and requiring MLFL rather than MAIL.

today: This note updates RFC 542 and RFC 607. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: A Reply to RFC 607
sections.content: Ken Pogran (MIT-Multics) and N. Neigus (BBN-NET) respond to Mark Krilanovich and George Gregg, whose RFC 607 commented on the File Transfer Protocol defined in RFC 542. They do not agree with everything but think each point deserves thought. Each numbered paragraph here answers the same-numbered paragraph there.
sections.plainLanguage: They go down a list of someone else's ideas, answering each in order.

sections.title: Modes, Command Length and Handshaking
sections.content:
The passive instruction applies only to the next file transfer. The authors welcome a way to change one's mind and suggest 200 MODE CHANGED TO ACTIVE or 200 MODE IS ALREADY ACTIVE. Some servers that listen after PASV cannot see ACTV on the control connection, so a user-FTP should send a SYNC sequence first.

They agree that commands should always be four characters. For transfers, the user listens on the data connection first. The server then checks the file and, if fine, tries to open the connection, answering 250 or an error (450, 451, 455, 457 or 454). A server that cannot watch both connections needs a timeout, no shorter than fifteen seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as agreeing the order of a handshake so everyone knows who speaks first and how long to wait.

sections.title: Replies and Reply Codes
sections.content:
Servers should return success to irrelevant commands such as ACCT and ALLO, and the authors want "must" instead of "should". They give Multics limits: Telnet lines 256, user names 32, passwords 8, pathnames 168.

They reject a change to multi-line replies. A fourth character of a hyphen starts a multi-line reply, and a line with the three digits and a space ends it. This lets a server reuse directory-listing code. Nested replies need not carry reply codes. They also disagree that any 2xx means success, preferring a redesign of the whole scheme, and suggest merging 000 and 020 so that 300 means ready.
sections.plainLanguage: Replies start with a number, and a dash after it means more lines are coming, like a letter that says to be continued.

sections.title: Login, Data Edge Cases and Mail
sections.content:
Data between the last end-of-record marker and end-of-file should be discarded. They propose removing the 331 reply, so that a server needing an account forgets the request and returns a 4XX reply, instead of holding a command in abeyance.

For mail, they note line-length trouble and that Multics uses at-sign as its line-kill character, which broke TENEX users' USERNAME@HOST addresses. They propose that mail-sending automata must use MLFL rather than MAIL.
sections.plainLanguage: They tidy up odd cases, like what to do with leftover bits, and ask programs to send mail the safer way.

references.text: Krilanovich and Gregg, Comments on the File Transfer Protocol, RFC 607.
